summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application (sqli package: views, routes, middlewares, DAOs, auth, templates, services) plus config and migrations. The app is riddled with high-impact, reachable flaws: a classic SQL injection in Student.create, unsalted MD5 password hashing, CSRF protection disabled, global Jinja2 autoescaping turned off leading to stored XSS, non-HttpOnly session cookies, missing authorization on state-changing endpoints, and verbose error/debug output that leaks internals. Overall risk is critical.

findings.title: SQL injection in Student.create via unparameterized name interpolation
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python string formatting (% operator) on the attacker-supplied `name`, then executes it without parameters. The value flows directly from an untrusted HTTP source: POST /students/ -> views.students (sqli/views.py:54-57) -> Student.create(conn, data['name']). Any anonymous user can inject arbitrary SQL (e.g. name = `x'); DROP TABLE students;--` or stacked UNION/subquery payloads). There is no authentication requirement on the handler and CSRF middleware is disabled, so this is directly reachable and exploitable. This is the headline vulnerability of the app; note every other DAO method correctly uses parameterized queries, so this one is the distinct offender.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})\nawait cur.execute(q)  # no params -> value already concatenated into SQL text
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query exactly like the other DAOs: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into SQL text.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 in User.check_password
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash against md5(password). MD5 is a fast, broken hash with no salt and no work factor, so a leaked users table (reachable via the SQLi above) is trivially cracked with rainbow tables / GPU brute force. The migration seeds users with md5('superadmin'), md5('password'), etc. (migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13), confirming the stored format. This affects the login flow in views.index:41.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()\n# storage: VALUES ('Super', NULL, 'Admin', 'superadmin', md5('superadmin'), TRUE)
findings.recommendation: Hash with a slow, salted KDF (argon2id or bcrypt), e.g. argon2.PasswordHasher, and compare with a constant-time verify. Rehash on next login during migration.

findings.title: CSRF protection disabled application-wide
findings.description: The csrf_middleware is commented out of the middleware chain, so no POST endpoint validates the _csrf_token that the templates render. A working token-checking middleware exists (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) but is never installed. Every state-changing route (login POST /, /students/, /courses/, /courses/{id}/review, /students/{id}/evaluate/{id}, /logout/) can be triggered cross-site. An attacker page can force a logged-in admin's browser to create records, submit reviews, or assign marks.
findings.evidence:
middlewares=[session_middleware,
    # csrf_middleware,
    error_middleware,
]  # csrf_middleware never added
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware list and ensure all POST forms submit the token (they already render it). Also set SameSite on the session cookie.

findings.title: Jinja2 autoescaping disabled causing stored XSS
findings.description: setup_jinja is configured with autoescape=False, so all template variables render raw HTML unless an explicit |e filter is applied (most are not). User-controlled data is stored and reflected unescaped: review_text submitted via POST /courses/{id}/review (views.py:129) is rendered in sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22 as `{{ review.review_text }}`; student names (students.jinja2:16) and course title/description (course.jinja2:14-15) are likewise unescaped. An anonymous user can store `<script>...</script>` in a review and execute JavaScript in every visitor's session, including admins.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli','templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False)\n# course.jinja2:22  {{ review.review_text }}  (no |e)
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=select_autoescape(['jinja2','html']) or autoescape=True) and only mark explicitly trusted content safe. Do not rely on scattered |e filters.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (students/courses/review/evaluate)
findings.description: The evaluate handler assigns grades (Mark.create) with no authentication or authorization check, even though the UI gates the evaluate form behind `auth_user.is_admin` (course.jinja2:41). The authorize() decorator (sqli/utils/auth.py:12) is only applied to logout; every other mutating route is unprotected. Consequently any anonymous user can POST to /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} to forge marks, and the same missing-check pattern lets anyone create students (views.py:54-57), create courses (views.py:86-90), and post reviews (views.py:119-129). Reported here on evaluate as the clearest privilege violation.
findings.evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points'])  # no @authorize(ensure_admin=True); only logout uses the decorator
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize() / @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to all mutating handlers (evaluate, students POST, courses POST, review POST) and enforce server-side that the client cannot perform privileged actions it is not entitled to.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: The RedisStorage session cookie is created with httponly=False, making the session identifier readable from JavaScript. Combined with the stored XSS from disabled autoescaping, an attacker's injected script can exfiltrate any visitor's (including admin's) session cookie and hijack the account.
findings.recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default), and also set secure=True and samesite='Lax'/'Strict' for the session cookie.

findings.title: Exception internals leaked to users via debug mode and 50x template
findings.description: The server error template renders `{{ error.__dict__ }}` directly to the response, dumping the full internal state of the raised exception to any user who triggers a 500. Together with Application(debug=True) in sqli/app.py:24, this exposes stack/exception details that aid attackers in exploiting the other flaws (e.g. SQL errors revealing schema). Reachable by anyone who can cause an unhandled error.
findings.recommendation: Render a generic message to users, log details server-side with a correlation id, and disable debug (debug=False) in production.
